title: 5 Theory of Attachment and Place Attachment

findings.antecedent: Forced dislocation from place of residence (e.g., urban redevelopment)
findings.consequent: Reactions resembling sorrow after loss of a loved one, interruption in sense of continuity, fragmentation of spatial and group identity
findings.quote: revealed that the reactions of a large number of interviewees resembled the sorrow experienced after the loss of a loved one. Fried postulated that the forced transfer from the place of residence represented an interruption in the individuals' sense of continuity, in that it involved the fragmentation of two essential components of identity, namely spatial identity and group identity, which are associated with strong affective elements.

findings.consequent: Feeling of belongingness to the place of residence, sorrow at moving out of the community
findings.quote: In particular, length of residence seems to be closely linked both to the feeling of belongingness and to the sorrow at moving out of the community – both of which are also age-linked

findings.antecedent: Congruity between individual needs and physical/social resources of the environment
findings.quote: The model's core concept is the congruity between needs and the physical and social resources of the environment: in positive cases attachment is developed, whereas in the case of incongruity, the individuals will either not form attachments or be repulsed.

findings.consequent: Increased presence of symptoms of malaise
findings.quote: a high index of mobility is associated with an increased presence of symptoms of malaise
one such undesirable aspect could be lack of attachment, since such a lack is a significant indicator of future mobility.

findings.antecedent: Stronger and healthier attachment to a main interpersonal figure
findings.consequent: More likely to have secondary interpersonal attachments
findings.quote: It seems even that the stronger and healthier the attachment to the main figure, the more likely there are to be secondary attachments (Bowlby, 1969, p. 308).

findings.antecedent: Unfavorable environmental conditions (e.g., abuse, ill treatment)
findings.quote: The relationship with the attachment figure tends to persist also under unfavourable environmental conditions, such as abuse and ill treatment

findings.consequent: Greater capacity to adapt models to the environmental situation
findings.quote: The capacity to adapt the models to fit the environmental situation is greater in the case of healthy development, that is of secure attachment

findings.consequent: Feelings of affection for a place
findings.quote: The feeling of affection for a place would develop in individuals whose positively-valenced knowledge of the environment in question largely exceeds the negatively-valenced knowledge.

findings.consequent: Preclusion of affection or cause of aversion
findings.quote: places normally associated with a positive affect can also preclude the emergence of any feelings of affection or even cause aversion when they threaten the individual's identity.

findings.consequent: Greater desire for stability in adulthood
findings.quote: a high degree of mobility during childhood is associated with a greater desire for stability in adulthood

findings.antecedent: Modality of arrival in neighborhood (free vs. compulsory choice)
findings.quote: the modality of arrival in the neighbourhood, or the perception of whether it was a free or a compulsory choice, carries greater weight.

findings.antecedent: Unsatisfactory residential experiences during infancy and adolescence
findings.consequent: Negative long-term consequences on capacity to form attachments in adulthood
findings.quote: unsatisfactory residential experiences occurring during infancy and adolescence seem to have negative long-term consequences on the capacity to form attachments in adulthood

findings.consequent: Stronger feelings of attachment, better expression of individual identity
findings.quote: primary territories are better able to express individual identity and are characterised by stronger feelings of attachment

findings.consequent: Facilitation of attachment to the neighborhood, development of secondary territoriality
findings.quote: the street layout can facilitate attachment to the neighbourhood and thus the development of a secondary territoriality.

findings.consequent: Relaxation, security, recuperation from stresses of the outside world
findings.quote: safe haven, the home is a safe haven where the resident can relax, feel secure, and recuperate from the stresses of the outside world

findings.consequent: Preponderance of the need for security and protection
findings.quote: we may conjecture that the need for security and protection preponderates during certain stages of life (e.g. childhood and old age)

findings.antecedent: Impaired physical resources and diminished capacity to adapt (elderly)
findings.consequent: Retreat from novel environments, seeking security, stronger attachment to home/neighborhood
findings.quote: Impaired physical resources and the diminished capacity to adapt spatial behaviour patterns to changes in the immediate environment contribute to making the elderly retreat from the novel and seek security. Similarly, the stronger attachment to the neighbourhood found among the lower classes might be accounted for by the continued activation of stress reducing behaviours connected with poverty of resources (Fried 2000).
